![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/0e5257867dae67451500793687a2da24ee31a73a17c691d8d8a6dcded46e8993.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the three-quarters of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(3,0),$ as shown above.
worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t){e}^{1-{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u={cos}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =-9{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,(-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}[{e}^{1}-{e}^{0}] \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\cdot (e-1) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(e-1)\end{aligned}
$$
